## Statistics workshops for graduate students

Annual workshops for graduate students in Human Development and Family Sciences
at UT Austin, run through the departmental statistics committee.

::: {.course}
**AI-assisted data analysis: Vibe coding with Positron** [· January 2026]{.meta}

Working with an AI assistant inside a real analysis project: what it is good
at, where it fails silently, and the verification habits that make it safe on
research code.

::: {.entry-links}
[Slides](files/workshops/2026/vibe-coding-slides.pptx)
[Script](files/workshops/2026/pilot.R)
:::
:::

::: {.course}
**Data wrangling with R** [· January 2025]{.meta}

Reshaping, merging, and cleaning messy data.

::: {.entry-links}
[Materials](files/workshops/2025/data-wrangling.Rmd)
:::
:::

::: {.course}
**Plotting figures with R** [· January 2024]{.meta}

Publication-quality figures in ggplot2, including legends, facets, fonts, and
export settings that survive a journal's production process.

::: {.entry-links}
[Slides](files/workshops/2024/figures-slides.pptx)
[Script](files/workshops/2024/figures-lecture.R)
:::
:::

::: {.course}
**Basic data analysis with R** [· January 2023]{.meta}

A first course for students who had only used SPSS: projects, scripts,
reproducibility, descriptives, and regression.

::: {.entry-links}
[R basics](files/workshops/2023/00-r-basics.R)
[Analysis with bruceR](files/workshops/2023/01-basic-analysis-bruceR.R)
:::
:::

In development: a workshop on the concepts underneath AI-assisted research,
covering tokens, context windows, agents, and the command line, for researchers
with no computing background.

Datasets are not posted. The examples use participant data that is not mine to
distribute, and I am rebuilding the exercises on synthetic data.

## AI and computational methods

I am an advanced user and teacher of computational methods rather than a methods
developer. What I do is bring these tools into applied developmental research
and teach other researchers to use them without losing rigour.

- Recurrent neural network models of student learning trajectories, with
  feature-importance analyses, compared against conventional growth models.
- Teaching AI-assisted analysis, through the January 2026 workshop and the
  concepts workshop in development.
- Verification: a generated number is a hypothesis until it has been re-derived
  from source output.

<figcaption>Engagement and the course overall are the two lowest items, while
the instructor-facing items are the highest.</figcaption>
:::

Three things I would do differently, and will.

**Know the program setting.** HDF 315L is a lower-division course, so I designed
it for lower-division students. Almost everyone who enrolled was a junior or
senior, with one exception. That mismatch drove the pacing and the level of
scaffolding.

**Replace the group activities.** They work in the large lecture sections I had
assisted. In a room of nine upper-level students they produced quiet compliance
rather than discussion. I am moving to structured pair work and written-first
protocols, where everyone commits to an answer before anyone speaks.

**Talk to students earlier.** I waited for questions and read a quiet room as an
understanding room. A start-of-semester survey on background and goals, plus
short mid-unit check-ins, replaces that inference.

<figcaption>The two weaknesses were specific and fixable. Presence was the
larger one: in the first large lecture, the single most common comment was that
students had not realised the course had a teaching assistant.</figcaption>
:::

Feedback quality and responsiveness held across every appointment, from a
220-student lecture to a six-student seminar. The two criticisms were
concentrated early. Being visible in a large room is a skill I did not have in
2022 and had to build deliberately: arriving before class, introducing myself,
announcing office hours rather than posting them, and staying afterwards. By
Fall 2024 the complaint had nearly disappeared and availability had become the
most praised thing about my teaching.

Grading followed the same pattern. Early comments described my marking as harsh
and inconsistent with the instructor's. The fix was calibration rather than
leniency: agreeing standards with the instructor in advance, marking against a
rubric, and explaining what a deduction was for. Occasional comments still call
me exacting, which I am comfortable with now that it is predictable.

The one thing still open is reach. In every cohort a few students report little
contact, while others describe the same semester as the most support they have
had. Availability is not outreach.

## Mentoring

I have supervised undergraduate research projects in the Perry and Benner labs,
and trained graduate and undergraduate assistants in physiological data
collection and preprocessing: RSA acquisition with Mindware, behavioural coding
with Mangold Interact, and the cleaning pipelines that follow.
